title: The recorder that ran ahead of the water
public_context: An oral-history interview recalls a keeper's work at a fictional tidal station. The setting includes a gauge room, paper charts, handwritten logs and mechanical instruments, and the account is part of a station archive of operator memories. The recorded conversation was later transcribed for the collection.
source_title: Interview with former station keeper Olan Vey, North Shoal gauge room
source_text:
Olan Vey remembers the recorder as a wooden box with a brass drum that turned under a sheet of gridded paper. A float in the outer well moved a cord, and the cord lifted the pen arm as the water rose. Every midnight the keeper wound the drum clock and wrote the time on the margin. The machine did not print a date; the date came from the keeper's pencil and the paper strip's drawer label. Vey says the system worked well until a hard frost stiffened the cord.

During the frost of Year Nine, the pen line flattened while the outside tide marks kept climbing. Vey first thought the water had stopped rising, but when the float well was opened after dawn, a thin skin of ice held the float below the surface. He cleared the well with a wooden scoop and the arm moved again. He did not use a metal hook because it could scratch the float and leave a false notch in later traces. The morning logbook records the ice, the scoop and the time when the pen resumed.

The paper chart and the logbook were stored in separate drawers because the chart could be removed from the drum only after the day's turn ended. Vey says the chart clock ran eleven minutes ahead of the station's wall clock by the end of the cold week. He wrote both times on the chart sleeve and drew a small bracket between them. The archive kept the chart with the original pen line, even where the line was flat, and filed the logbook beside it rather than drawing a corrected curve over the gap.

Vey recalls that a later keeper fitted a warmer cover over the cord passage. He never saw a second float recorder in the room. Near the end of the interview, Vey tapped the paper chart and said its value was that a reader could compare the machine trace with the keeper's notes, not that the line alone answered every question. He asked the archivist to keep the sleeve beside the logbook on the gauge-room shelf.

licensed_inferences.rationale: The outside tide marks kept climbing while ice held the float below the surface, interrupting the float-cord-pen mechanism. The flat trace therefore cannot establish that the tide stopped rising.
